summary: Glean is a web tool that helps farmers in western Kansas choose crop rotations using 25 years of NASA and USDA data about their own field. Farms there pump from the Ogallala aquifer, which is running down: NASA’s GRACE satellites show regional water storage falling about 0.86 cm a year, and nearby wells are dropping up to 1.8 m a year. Glean replays a field’s current rotation and six alternatives on every day of real weather since 2000 (NASA POWER), using the field’s own soil, terrain and crop history and the standard FAO-56 crop water model. The farmer sets priorities and a pumping limit, and Glean shows the current rotation next to the three best fits. Each option explains why it was suggested, the evidence, benefits, information gaps and risks to check locally. Glean also shows the water similar neighbouring fields actually used (OpenET), a month-by-month risk calendar including Dust Bowl-style wind erosion, and an English/Spanish assistant whose every number is checked against the data. Glean supports a farmer’s judgement but doesn’t replace it.
details:
Glean: find the crop rotation that fits your field, backed by 25 years of NASA data

Live app: https://glean-farms.vercel.app

Code: https://github.com/mrudduni/Team-Brackets

The start page: three real fields near Garden City, Kansas, and the datasets behind them. (Image: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrudduni/Team-Brackets/main/docs/assets/glean-home.png)

The problem

Farms in southwest Kansas pump their irrigation water from the Ogallala aquifer, and it is running down. NASA's GRACE and GRACE-FO satellites show water stored underground in the region falling about 0.86 cm a year since 2002. USGS wells near our three demo fields show the water table dropping between 0.25 and 1.8 m a year. July heat hurts corn at pollination. The sandy soils that blew away in the Dust Bowl still blow when they lie bare in spring.

Farmers already weigh irrigated corn against dryland wheat, sorghum and fallow. What they rarely see is evidence for their own field: how each rotation would have done on its soil, through its droughts, with the water it can actually pump.

What Glean does

Glean is a decision-support web app. It replays a field's current rotation and six alternatives on every day of real weather since 2000, then puts the current rotation next to the three that best fit the farmer's priorities. As the challenge asks, every option explains why it was suggested, the evidence, the benefits, the information gaps and the risks to check locally. Glean never names a winner; it shows the trade-offs and the farmer decides.

  • Pick a field. Three real fields near Garden City: an irrigated centre pivot, a dryland wheat field and a sandy, wind-prone field.
  • See the field's story. The rotation it has actually grown (from USDA crop maps), its soil, how the local climate has shifted (1991–2020 vs 2016–2025) and the groundwater outlook.
  • Set priorities and limits. Five sliders (save water, income, steady income in bad years, soil health, erosion control), a seasonal pumping limit (0, 150, 300 or 450 mm) and the equipment and markets the farmer has.
  • Compare strategy cards. The current rotation plus the top three, each with five sections: Why it's suggested · What the data shows · Possible benefits · What we don't know · Check locally before switching.
  • Rotation Replay, 2000–2025. Irrigation needed, income, water-stress days and bare-soil days for every year, with the 2002, 2011, 2012 and 2022 droughts marked, plus a "hotter and drier" test (+1.5 °C, 15% less rain).
  • Field Calendar. Month by month: what is in the ground or when it lies bare, with 25-year odds of damaging heat, frost, dry spells, storms and strong wind.
  • Farms Like Yours. Neighbouring fields on similar soil that already farm differently, with the water they really used, measured from satellites.
  • Ask about this field. A plain-language assistant in English and Spanish. Every number in its answer is checked against the field's data and tagged with its source.
  • How we know this. Sources, methods, validation results and a glossary on one page.

Field overview for the irrigated north pivot. Every panel names the dataset behind it. (Image: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrudduni/Team-Brackets/main/docs/assets/glean-field.png)

How it works:

What it shows: the irrigated north pivot

The hard trade-off is visible, not hidden: going dryland saves all of the pumping but cuts gross income sharply, while the alfalfa rotation keeps similar water use, leaves the soil bare on far fewer windy days and scores much higher on soil health. In Farms Like Yours, 30 of 150 neighbouring fields matched this one; the 11 that already grow corn, wheat and sorghum used a median 849 mm of water a year by OpenET satellite measurement, against 932 mm for the 12 continuous-corn fields.

How we checked it

Modelled crop water use was compared with OpenET satellite estimates over 56 growing-season months per field: +0.9% difference on the irrigated pivot, +6.5% on the sandy field and −29.6% on the dryland field, where weeds and volunteer wheat in fallow years use more water than our bare-soil model assumes. The app shows these results as trust badges next to the numbers, including the weak one.

Benefits

  • Field-specific evidence: results come from the farmer's own soil, terrain, crop history and 25 years of local weather, not regional averages.
  • Drought stress test: farmers see each option's worst years, not only its average.
  • Water in real units: irrigation in mm and inches per season, easy to compare with a water-right limit.
  • Wind erosion in view: bare days in windy months, weighted by how easily the soil blows, a risk most rotation tools ignore.
  • Honest uncertainty: every card lists what we don't know and what to check with a K-State Research and Extension agent.
  • Accessible: plain language, English and Spanish, works on a phone, colours checked for colour blindness.

Intended impact

Kansas is asking irrigators to use less water from a falling aquifer. Switching rotations is one of the few levers a farmer controls, but it is a costly bet without evidence. Glean turns NASA and USDA records into a transparent, field-level comparison a farmer can discuss with their family, lender or extension agent. The same pipeline works for any field in the western US where these datasets exist; the three Finney County fields are the demonstration.

What makes it creative

  1. Replay instead of averages. Each rotation lives through 26 real seasons, droughts included.
  2. Neighbours as evidence. Satellite water use of similar nearby fields that already farm differently, labelled as observational, with the number of fields always shown.
  3. A Dust Bowl lens. Wind-erosion exposure for the sandy soils of southwest Kansas.
  4. An assistant that can't make up numbers silently. Every figure is checked against the data and tagged with its source; anything unbacked is flagged.

Tools and technologies

  • Data and model: Python 3.11 (pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas, xarray, pyet), pytest.
  • Web: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Recharts, Zod, hosted on Vercel.
  • Assistant: Groq and Google Gemini through an OpenAI-compatible API, with a number checker and an LLM-as-judge review of cached answers.
  • Collaboration: GitHub, a shared data contract between the four roles (data, model, frontend, design and content).

Factors we considered

  • Trust over persuasion: no winner is named, wording says "may" and "estimated", and limits such as missing pest data, costs and constant prices are listed on every card.
  • The farmer's real constraints: pumping limits, equipment, livestock or hay buyers and local markets decide which options appear.
  • Scientific validity: standard FAO methods, published crop parameters, and validation against independent satellite data.
  • Who reads it: large type and high contrast for phones outdoors, and Spanish for western Kansas's many Spanish-speaking farm workers.
  • Supports, never replaces: Glean supports the farmer's judgement and local expertise. It does not replace them.

Team Brackets: Himal Garg (lead), Rishi Garg, Aditya, Khushal Goel, Mrudduni J. Modha, Parisha Gupta.
